implementationPlan.coreSkill: Trace a strong feeling back to the story behind it, then check that story against what really happened.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking someone did something on purpose to hurt me, I name that thought as a story and say the plain facts next to it.
When I sit down to answer a message that made me angry, I write down the story I'm telling before I type a single word.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, recall one moment today when you felt annoyed. Write the facts on one line and the story you told yourself on the next.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, pick the moment you felt most angry or hurt. Walk it backward in order: what you did, what you felt, the story you told, and the plain facts.

chapters.title: Start With What You Saw, Not What You Suspect
chapters.hook: You're holding the receipt and you're sure what it means. Say what it means first, and you'll get a fight, not an answer.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think the honest move is to get straight to the point and say what they think is going on. Actually, opening with what you saw works better, because facts are hard to argue with, while a conclusion puts them on the defense.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you must say something hard, open with the plain facts before you share what you think they mean.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell one person today about a small thing that's been bugging you, starting with what you saw, then what you think it means.

memorableLines.text: Show what you saw before you say what you suspect.

breakdown.fastRead:
The cash drawer at Tomás's bike repair shop has come up forty dollars short twice this week. Both nights, his mechanic Anneke locked up. He plans to open Saturday by telling her he knows she's been taking from the till. If he's wrong, he loses his best mechanic.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler warn against that opening. It leads with your story, meaning what you've decided the facts mean. In one of their cases, Carole finds a charge from the Good Night Motel on the credit card bill. She decides her husband, Bob, is having an affair. Accusing him outright would put him on the defense. The better start is the charge itself, a line on a bill both can see. Then she shares her worry and lets him explain. Facts, the authors say, are the least insulting part of your view and the hardest to argue with. They show how you reached your story.

On Saturday, Tomás lays the cash slips on the counter. He tells her the drawer was forty short on Tuesday and Thursday, and that she closed both nights. He says he's worried money is going missing, and asks how it looks to her. Anneke starts counting back through her shifts. Once you open with what you saw before what you think it means, your worry gets a hearing instead of a fight.

The cash drawer at Tomás's bike repair shop has come up forty dollars short twice this week. Both nights, his mechanic Anneke locked up. He plans to open Saturday by telling her he knows she's been taking from the till. It feels honest and direct. But if he's wrong, he loses his best mechanic over forty dollars. If he's right, she will just deny it, and the money never gets talked about.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler see this pull in almost everyone facing a risky talk. People lead with their story, meaning what they've decided the facts mean. The story is the part that hurts, so it's the part people rush to say. It's also the part most likely to make the other person go quiet or hit back. The authors teach STATE, a five-step way to say hard things honestly and safely, and its first step is to share your facts. Facts, they say, are the least insulting part of your view, the hardest to argue with and the most persuasive. Your story grew out of them, so they show how you got there.

One of their cases is Carole, who finds a charge from the Good Night Motel, close to home, on the credit card bill. She decides that her husband, Bob, is having an affair. The authors set two openings side by side. In one, she accuses him outright, and he can only defend himself. In the other, she starts with the charge itself, a line on a bill they can both look at. Then she tells him what she fears it means and gives him room to explain. Her worry still gets said. It simply comes after the fact that led to it, so Bob can follow her thinking.

On Saturday, Tomás lays the cash slips on the counter. He tells her the drawer was forty short on Tuesday and Thursday, and that she closed both nights. He says he's worried money is going missing, and asks how it looks to her. He hasn't hidden his worry. He has only put it after the slips that caused it. Anneke has no accusation to deny, only numbers to look at, and she starts counting back through her shifts. Once you open with what you saw before what you think it means, your worry gets a hearing instead of a fight.

The cash drawer at Tomás's bike repair shop has come up forty dollars short twice this week. Both nights, his mechanic Anneke locked up. He plans to open Saturday by telling her he knows she's been taking from the till. He has gone over it all morning, and it feels honest and direct. If he's wrong, he loses his best mechanic over forty dollars. If he's right, she will just deny it.

Getting straight to the point seems like the honest move. The trouble is which point. Tomás never saw Anneke take anything. He saw two short counts and two closing shifts, and he joined them into a conclusion. Once he opens with that conclusion, she has two choices. She can admit to stealing, or she can defend her name. Even an innocent person gets loud at that moment, and the forty dollars drop out of the talk.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler studied how people handle talks like this, at work and at home. When the stakes run high, most either hold back what they think or say it like a blow. The authors' way out is a skill called STATE, a five-step way to say hard things honestly and safely. The first three steps are what you say. You share your facts, tell your story, meaning what you've decided the facts mean, and ask how the other person sees it. The last two are how you say it. You offer your story as a story rather than a fact, and you make it safe for others to disagree.

Facts come first, and the authors give their reasons. Facts are the least insulting part of your view. They are the hardest to argue with and the most persuasive. A count on a cash slip is just a count. A story is a judgment about someone, and judgments make people defend themselves. Facts also show your path. Your worry grew out of what you saw, so laying out what you saw lets the other person see how you got there.

The authors warn that pushing only makes people push back.

examples.title: A market pitch moved to the back
examples.scenario: Ximena sells hand-dyed yarn from a stall at a Saturday market. For three weeks running, the market manager has moved her pitch from the front gate to a back corner beside the bins, and her takings have halved. A new honey stall now sits in her old spot. She's sure he's making room for a friend, and she's walking to his hut to say so.
examples.whatToDo: Start with the three Saturdays, the corner by the bins and your halved takings. Then say what you're starting to suspect, and ask what changed.
examples.whyItMatters: Dates and takings are hard to dispute, so the manager can explain the move instead of defending himself.

examples.title: The pill box that moved to a drawer
examples.scenario: Last Sunday, Babajide saw that his mother's weekly pill box was still full from Monday to Wednesday. He said, "You've stopped taking your blood pressure pills, haven't you?" She snapped that she wasn't a child and changed the subject. The pill box has since moved from the kitchen counter to her bedroom drawer, and now he can't tell whether she takes them.
examples.whatToDo: Tell her plainly what you saw: last Sunday, Monday to Wednesday were still full, and now the box has moved to her drawer. Then say you're worried, and ask what's going on with the pills.
examples.whyItMatters: Full slots are something she can explain, like a side effect or a lost refill, without being called careless.

examples.title: One blank section, two days to go
examples.scenario: Tariq, fifteen, shares a history project with Rosalind, and it's due Friday. Wanting to start with facts, he told her at lunch, "Fact: you haven't done anything for this project." Rosalind rolled her eyes, said that wasn't true, and walked off. Her section of their shared document is still blank, and his three messages to her show as read.
examples.whatToDo: Open the shared document together and point at the blank section and the three read messages. Then say you're worried about Friday, and ask where she's stuck.
examples.whyItMatters: Doing nothing was his judgment of her. A blank page and read messages are things she can see for herself.

questions.prompt: Your sister borrowed your car and brought it back with the tank nearly empty and a fresh scrape on the bumper. You plan to start with, "You clearly don't care about my things." What's the trap in that opening?
choices: It opens with what you've decided, so she has to defend herself first.
It raises this too soon, before you have both had time to cool down.
It mixes two problems when the scrape needs its own talk.
questions.explanation: Saying she doesn't care is a conclusion she has to fight. The empty tank and the scrape are things you can both look at. Waiting to cool down would not change how that line lands.

questions.prompt: A team lead at a print shop tells a staff member, "Your last three orders went out after the Friday deadline. I'm starting to wonder if you've got too much on. What's going on?" What is the most likely result?
choices: He feels the list is an ambush and argues about each late order.
He promises to be on time but stays guarded around the lead.
He can check the dates himself, so he explains what's behind them.
questions.explanation: Late orders are something he can check, so there is nothing to defend and room to explain. The dates would only feel like an ambush if they came after an accusation.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My brother keeps borrowing my tools, and I'm sure he's lending them to his mates. Tonight I'm telling him he's using me." What's your best reply?
choices: "Start with which tools came back late and when, then share your suspicion."
"Leave your suspicion out of it and just ask him to return the tools."
"Ask him straight out who he has been lending them to."
questions.explanation: Which tools came back late, and when, are things your brother can check, and they show how your suspicion grew. Asking who he lends them to already assumes he does.

questions.prompt: A choir member emails the choir leader, "My name wasn't on the solo list for spring or summer, though I sang solos all last year. I'm wondering if my voice has slipped. Could we talk?" The leader calls back within the hour. Why did the note get such a quick, warm answer?
choices: The worry was put gently, so the leader felt sorry and wanted to help.
The question at the end let the leader steer the talk.
The leader could see the two lists, so the worry made sense.
questions.explanation: Two solo lists are hard to argue with, and they show how the singer reached that worry. A gentle tone alone would not have shown the leader why.

questions.prompt: You and a business partner run a small dog-walking company. This week you spotted two new clients on the schedule that he booked without telling you, and you're sure he's planning to go solo. You're about to call him. How do you open the call?
choices: Say plainly you know he's planning to leave, so nobody plays games.
Point to the two new names you didn't book, then share your worry.
Open by saying how much the business means to you, to keep it warm.
questions.explanation: Two names on the schedule are something he can look at and explain. Saying you know he's leaving hands him a conclusion to fight, and he may have another reason.

questions.prompt: A pharmacist sees her coworker's breaks ran twenty minutes long on four days this week. At the counter, she tells him the four dates and times, then stops and waits. He says, "Okay?" and goes back to the shelves. Where did her approach slip?
choices: She raised it at the counter, where others could overhear.
She gave him the times but didn't say why they worried her.
She listed all four days, which made it feel like she was keeping score.
questions.explanation: The times opened the talk well, but she still had to say what she thought they meant. Without her worry they were just numbers. Four days he can check are fair, not score-keeping.

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner sees in the booking system that his head waiter cancelled six large bookings this month. He opens with, "You're turning customers away to make your shifts easier." What most likely happens next?
choices: The talk turns into a fight about his motives, not the six bookings.
He owns up, since all six cancellations are sitting right there in the system.
He's stung, but the blunt words make him take it seriously.
questions.explanation: Leading with his motive gives the waiter something to deny, so the six bookings get lost. Having the proof in the system doesn't help when it never comes up first.

reviewCards.front: Why does opening a hard talk with what you saw work better than opening with what you think it means?
reviewCards.back: What you saw is something both of you can check, so there's little to fight. It also shows how you reached your worry, so it makes sense to them.

reviewCards.front: Before you say what you think something means, first say ...
reviewCards.back: ... the plain facts you saw or heard, in words the other person could check for themselves.

reviewCards.front: A parent says, "You've been lying about where you go after school." The teen storms off, and the real issue never comes up. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The parent opened with a judgment. Starting with what they actually saw would have given the teen something to explain instead of something to deny.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: how should you open a hard talk, and why?
reviewCards.back: Lead with what you saw, then what you think it means. Facts are hard to argue with, and they show how you got to your worry.

reviewCards.front: A coworker has missed your last three shared deadlines, and you're starting to think they've stopped caring about the project.
reviewCards.back: Open with the three deadlines and their dates. Then say you're starting to wonder about their interest, and ask how they see it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Laying out what you saw or heard before offering your own reading of it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself opening with what I've decided someone did, I stop, say only what I saw or heard, and then share my worry.
When I get home from work still annoyed about something someone did, I jot down only what I saw or heard, before deciding what to say.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tonight, pick one worry you've been sitting on. Write two lines on paper, one for what you actually saw or heard and one for what you think it means.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, look back at one hard talk you had. Check whether you led with what you saw or with what you'd decided, and rewrite your first line so the facts come first.

chapters.title: Find the Story Behind the Blow-Up
chapters.hook: Your daughter storms off after you criticize her new boyfriend. Arguing about him feels right. But the fight is rarely about him.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to calm someone's anger or argue the point they just shouted. But you get further by asking what they saw and what they made of it, because their feelings grow out of a story they haven't told you yet.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When someone blows up or goes silent, ask about the facts and story behind their feelings.
chapters.tryThisNow: At dinner tonight, ask one person at the table what they saw today that bothered them, then say their answer back.

memorableLines.text: Every blow-up rides on a story. Ask for the story first.

breakdown.fastRead:
When someone you care about blows up or goes silent, what do you go after first? Most of us calm the feeling or argue about whatever they shouted. Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler point further back. They say everyone walks a path to action: you see something, tell yourself a story about it, feel what it stirs up, then act. The outburst is only the last step.

Their example is Wendy, a teenager whose new boyfriend, Doug, worries her parent. When the parent scolds her, she blows up and pulls away. So the parent apologizes and gets curious. They ask how things look from her side. They name the feelings they see on her face. They retell her story in their own words. When she still holds back, they offer a best guess. The authors call these four moves AMPP: ask, mirror, paraphrase, prime. Finally Wendy admits she has felt unnoticed at home, and Doug pays attention to her.

The fight was never really about Doug. Arguing about him was the wrong fight. Soothing her would have left her story hidden, still steering her. Hearing her story is not agreeing with it. Stop soothing the feeling or arguing the topic, and ask what the other person saw and the story they made of it.

breakdown.fullRead:
When someone you care about blows up or goes silent, what do you go after first? Most of us calm the feeling or argue about whatever they shouted. Both feel like the grown-up thing to do. Both skip the part that matters most.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler point further back. They say everyone walks a path to action: you see something, tell yourself a story about it, feel what it stirs up, then act. Feelings don't appear from nowhere. They grow out of the story, and the story grows out of what someone saw or heard. So the shouting or the silence is only the last step. To change it, you have to go back toward where it started.

When stakes are high and feelings run strong, the authors say most people fall into silence or violence. Silence means holding back what you really think. Violence, in their sense, means pushing, mocking or forcing your view on others. Either way, the real story stays out of sight. People act on their own stories, and those stories may rest on facts you never knew. Calm the feeling, and the story stays hidden, still steering them. Argue the topic, and you fight about the wrong thing.

So the authors ask you to start with the right attitude. Be curious about what the other person saw and what it meant to them. Be patient, and don't rush them. Sincere interest makes it safe for someone to say what they have been carrying. Then the authors give four moves for drawing the story out, and their example uses all four.

Their example is Wendy, a teenager whose new boyfriend, Doug, worries her parent. When the parent scolds her, she blows up and pulls away. So the parent apologizes and gets curious instead of pushing harder. The parent's first move is to ask. They invite her to say how things look from her side, and they mean the question. Next they mirror, calmly naming the feelings they can see in her face and hear in her voice. That lets her know someone is paying attention to how she feels.

Then they paraphrase, retelling her story in their own words. A paraphrase isn't a parrot. It shows the story arrived, and it invites her to go on. When she still holds back, they prime. The name comes from priming an old hand pump, where you pour in a little water to get the flow started. Here the water is a best guess at what she might be thinking. The authors call the four moves together AMPP: ask, mirror, paraphrase, prime.

Bit by bit, Wendy admits what is underneath. She has felt unnoticed at home, and Doug pays attention to her. The fight was never really about Doug. Arguing about him would have kept the real issue buried. Soothing her would have quieted the feeling and left the story steering her. Hearing her story out is not agreeing with it, either. When your turn to speak comes, the authors suggest three steps. Agree where you do, add what the other person left out, and compare views rather than calling theirs wrong. That turn comes after the story is out. Stop soothing the feeling or arguing the topic, and ask what the other person saw and the story they made of it.

examples.title: Sharp words at the trailhead
examples.scenario: Anya runs a Saturday hiking club. At the trailhead she announces a longer route, and Dario, who usually jokes all morning, says, "Whatever, you always decide anyway," then walks off to retie his boots. He has hiked with her for years. Anya feels the sting, and part of her wants to list every reason the new route is better. She walks over to him.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the route aside. Ask him what he's noticed about how routes get chosen and how it looks to him, then say it back.
examples.whyItMatters: His jab comes from a story about how decisions get made, and a better route won't reach that story.

examples.title: A trainee who stopped asking questions
examples.scenario: Imogen trains new barbers at a barber school. Last week she pointed out an uneven cut, and her trainee Paulo muttered, "Fine, I'll redo it," then barely spoke. Imogen told him not to take it personally, then walked him through exactly why the cut went wrong. He nodded. Since then he hasn't asked a single question, and yesterday he skipped the session.
examples.whatToDo: Ask Paulo what he heard that day and what he made of it, then repeat his answer back in your own words.
examples.whyItMatters: Her kind words and her lesson both skipped his story, so whatever he decided that day is still steering him.

examples.title: One minute at the nursery gate
examples.scenario: It's pick-up time at the nursery where Wren works, and six parents are queued at the gate. Mateo's dad reaches the front, red in the face. "Second time this week he skipped lunch, and I heard it from him, not you." The parents behind him go quiet. Wren has about a minute before the line spills onto the pavement.
examples.whatToDo: Name the worry you see, ask what Mateo told him, and say it back in a sentence. Then offer a call tonight for the rest.
examples.whyItMatters: A minute spent on his story beats a quick reassurance that leaves his worry hidden until tomorrow's pick-up.

questions.prompt: Your partner has given one-word answers since you said yes to a weekend away with old school friends. Over tea, you ask what they've noticed lately and how it looks from their side, then repeat back what they say. What most likely happens next?
choices: They say it's fine, and the chill between you lasts for weeks.
They explain what they've seen, and the worry behind their silence comes out.
They hear your questions as blame and go even quieter with you than they were before.
questions.explanation: Asking what your partner has noticed and repeating it back invites the story behind their silence into the open. Your questions asked for their side instead of arguing about the weekend, so there is little to hear as blame.

questions.prompt: Your friend snaps that you only call when you need a favor, and hangs up. The next day she picks up when you ring. What's the best thing to say first?
choices: What have I done lately that made it feel that way to you?
That's not fair, I called you last month just to chat.
Let's just forget about it, okay? I really don't want this coming between us.
questions.explanation: Asking what you did that made it feel that way goes after what she saw and the story she built from it. Pointing to last month's call just argues the topic and leaves her story untouched.

questions.prompt: A boy shouts that chores in his house are a joke and storms to his room. His dad knocks, asks what he's noticed, and repeats it back. The boy says his sister gets out of every job. Why did asking work here?
choices: The questions gave him time to cool off before he talked.
His anger came from a story about fairness, and asking brought it out.
He felt sure his dad agreed with him, so he stopped needing to fight about it.
questions.explanation: The shouting grew from a story about his sister getting off easy, and asking brought it into the open. Repeating his words back isn't agreeing with them, so his dad hasn't given in on anything.

questions.prompt: Since your office moved to a new seating plan, a colleague has given you one-word replies. You asked what's up, said she seems annoyed, and repeated back the little she said. She still holds back. What's your next move?
choices: Leave it for now and give her a few days of space.
Offer a best guess, such as whether the new seating plan feels unfair.
Tell her plainly how her short replies have been making your own work harder.
questions.explanation: You've asked, named the feeling and repeated her words, and she still holds back. That's the moment for a best guess. Turning to your own work now pulls the talk away from her story.

questions.prompt: A mother's teenage son shouts that her new partner is ruining the family, then goes to his room. She decides not to ask what he means. Asking, she feels, would hand him a win. What trap is she caught in?
choices: Thinking she has to back her partner whenever her son attacks him.
Thinking she should first tell him how much his words have hurt her.
Thinking that hearing out his story would mean agreeing with it.
questions.explanation: Hearing his story out isn't the same as agreeing with it. If she never asks, she never learns what he saw or what he made of it, and that story keeps driving his anger.

questions.prompt: At a flower shop, an assistant snaps that she's always stuck with closing, then goes quiet. The owner tells her it's been a long week and sends her home early. What happens from here?
choices: She goes home calmer, but the closing complaint soon comes back.
She feels looked after, and closing shifts stop being a sore point.
She explains why closing bothers her, and they fix it.
questions.explanation: Sending her home early eases the feeling, but nobody asks what she has seen about who gets closing or what it means to her. The story behind the complaint stays hidden, so it returns.

questions.prompt: At a family dinner, your sister, who is planning her wedding, bursts out that nobody here listens to her. Then she stares at her plate. Which reply helps most?
choices: You must be feeling left out over all the wedding plans lately, right?
Why are you suddenly so angry with us?
Sounds like something's been building. What have you noticed lately?
questions.explanation: Naming what you see and asking what she has noticed starts her back toward the facts behind her outburst. A guess about the wedding comes too early, before she has had any chance to tell it herself.

reviewCards.front: When someone snaps at you or shuts down, before you answer what they said, you ask about ...
reviewCards.back: ... what they saw and the story they told themselves about it, since the feeling grows out of that story.

reviewCards.front: A coach benches a player, who storms off. She calls after him that she understands he's frustrated and he should take a breather. He sulks for weeks. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She eased the feeling but never asked what he saw or what he made of being benched, so that story kept running underneath.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: when someone blows up or goes silent, what do you go after first, and why?
reviewCards.back: Not their anger and not the topic. Go after what they saw and the story they built from it, because that story is what's driving the feeling.

reviewCards.front: Your neighbor shouts over the fence that your new shed blocks her light, then turns away. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Leave the shed debate for later. Ask what she's noticed since it went up and what it means for her, then say her answer back in your own words.

reviewCards.front: Why doesn't calming someone down fix an outburst?
reviewCards.back: The outburst comes from a story about what they saw. Calm the feeling and the story stays hidden, still steering them.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Drawing out the facts and the private story under someone's outburst or silence.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to dinner and someone at the table is unusually quiet, I ask what's been happening on their side and repeat back what they tell me.
When I catch myself thinking that someone is overreacting, I ask what they saw that I might have missed, before giving my side.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one person who snapped at you or went quiet this week. Before the day ends, ask them one question about what they saw, and say their answer back.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, recall one tense moment and note what you reached for first: soothing, arguing or asking what the other person saw. Aim for asking first by the weekend.

chapters.title: Agreeing Is Not Deciding: Name Who Makes the Call
chapters.hook: Everyone nodded as your meeting ended. A week later, a receipt arrives for something half of you never agreed to.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that once everyone nods, the matter is settled. The trouble is that each person nods to a different picture of what comes next, so say out loud who makes the final call and how.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a hard talk ends in agreement, say out loud how the final decision will be made and by whom.
chapters.tryThisNow: Send one message today about a plan you agreed on lately, naming who makes the final choice and how.

memorableLines.text: A nod agrees to the idea. Naming who decides settles the plan.

breakdown.fastRead:
A talk can end in warm agreement and still settle nothing. Everyone walks away sure it is closed, each with a different plan in mind. Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler show this with Cara and Rene, two people planning a trip together. They talk it over and agree a cruise sounds good. Then Rene picks one cruise and pays the deposit. Cara is upset. She said yes to the idea of a cruise, not to that ship or those dates.

The mistake is easy to make. Airing everyone's views takes effort, so the moment heads start nodding feels like the finish line. But talking freely and deciding are two separate steps. When nobody says how the choice gets made, each person assumes their own answer.

Before people leave, decide how you will decide, out loud. There are four ways. One person decides alone. One person or a small group decides after hearing the others. The group votes. Or everyone must honestly agree. For Cara and Rene, one question would have done it. Does one of us book, or do we both say yes to the exact trip first? With the second answer, the deposit waits for two yeses. An agreement holds when the people in it also agree, out loud, on who makes the final choice and how.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler show this with Cara and Rene, two people planning a trip together. They talk it over and agree a cruise sounds like a good idea. Then Rene picks one cruise and pays the deposit. Cara is upset. She said yes to the idea of a cruise, not to that ship or those dates.

Look at what each of them took away. For Rene, the talk ended with a go-ahead. For Cara, it ended with a first step, and the real choosing was still to come. They left the same talk holding two different pictures. Neither picture was said out loud, so neither could be checked.

The mistake is easy to make. Airing everyone's facts and feelings takes real effort, especially when the stakes are high and people disagree. When the heat finally drops and heads start nodding, the relief is huge. It feels like the finish line. So people smile, stand up and leave it there.

But talking freely and making a choice are two separate steps. The first gets every view on the table. The second turns those views into something that happens, and someone still has to do it. The authors warn that when this step stays vague, people end up with broken expectations, and work that was agreed to never gets done. Each person later feels let down by the others.

The fix is to decide how you will decide, before the talk breaks up. The authors give four ways. In command, the decision is made without involving the others. In consult, one person or a small group gathers ideas from others, then makes the call. In a vote, an agreed share of the group carries the decision. In consensus, everyone must honestly agree before anything moves. The trouble starts when people leave guessing which one is in play.

To choose among them, the authors suggest four questions. Who cares, meaning who will be affected and wants a say? Who knows, meaning who has the facts the choice needs? Who must agree, meaning whose support you need to carry it out? And how many people is it worth involving, so the choice is sound without pulling in more people than it needs? The answers usually point to one of the four ways.

For Cara and Rene, the questions answer themselves. Both are going on the trip, so both care, and both must be happy with it. That means the cruise itself needs two yeses. One question at the end would have done it. Does one of us book, or do we both say yes to the exact trip first? With the second answer, the deposit waits until one ship and one set of dates suit them both.

In any hard talk, the steps are short. Notice the moment people start nodding. Before anyone stands, say which of the four ways will settle the final choice and who holds it. Then name who does what by when, agree how you will follow up, write it down, and hold each other to it. An agreement holds when the people in it also agree, out loud, on who makes the final choice and how.

examples.title: When the sales meeting ends on 'we're agreed'
examples.scenario: Tanvi's sales team spends an hour in the office meeting room arguing about free shipping on small orders. By the end, everyone nods that something has to change. Her manager gathers up the printed sales reports and says, "Good, we're agreed." Nobody has said what the new rule is, or who sets it. Chairs start scraping back.
examples.whatToDo: Before anyone leaves, ask out loud who sets the new rule, and whether they decide alone or after hearing the team.
examples.whyItMatters: Otherwise someone posts a new rule on Friday, and the rest of the team feels the agreement was broken behind their backs.

examples.title: A recital yes, and a piece he dreads
examples.scenario: Oskar and his cello teacher spend a lesson talking about whether he is ready for the spring recital. At the end, he checks, "So we're agreed? I'm playing?" She smiles and says yes. A week later the printed program lists him playing a fast piece she chose. He had pictured choosing his own. Now he practices a piece he dreads.
examples.whatToDo: Before leaving a lesson that ends in a yes, ask who picks the piece and whether you get a say before it is printed.
examples.whyItMatters: His check only confirmed the idea of playing. Asking who chooses the piece settles the part they each pictured differently.

examples.title: The eldest sister with the agent's number
examples.scenario: Adaeze, her two younger brothers and their mother agree over Sunday lunch that the family house is now too big for one person. Adaeze is the eldest and has always been the one who sorts things out. She already has an estate agent's number saved. Asking the others who makes the final call feels like giving away the job that has always been hers.
examples.whatToDo: Before calling the agent, ask whether Mom decides after hearing her three children, or all four of them must agree.
examples.whyItMatters: Calling on a shared yes alone would leave her mother feeling a choice about her own home was made without her.

questions.prompt: After a meeting, a coworker tells you, "Everyone agreed we need a new scheduling app. I'll choose one tonight and set it up for the team." What is your best reply?
choices: Send round your meeting notes first, so nobody forgets what everyone actually said.
Great, send everyone the login as soon as it's set up.
Ask the team first whether you choose it or we all do.
questions.explanation: The team agreed it needs an app, not on which one. Asking who chooses keeps a surprise login from feeling like a broken deal. Meeting notes would only record the same vague yes.

questions.prompt: A swim club committee agrees practice times must change. Before the meeting ends, the chair says she will decide the new times after reading everyone's emails by Friday. Weeks later, nobody complains. Why did this work?
choices: Everyone knew who would choose and that their emails would count.
The chair knew more about swimming and practice times than anyone else.
The Friday deadline kept the debate from dragging on.
questions.explanation: The talk ended with everyone knowing the chair would choose after reading their emails, so nobody was surprised. The Friday date helped, but a deadline alone would not have told anyone who decides.

questions.prompt: You and your sister agree over coffee that your dad's seventieth birthday deserves a big party. She is already scrolling through venues on her phone. What do you do?
choices: Tell her which venue you like best before she goes and books one.
Leave her to it, trusting she knows what you both want.
Ask whether she picks the place or you two choose it together.
questions.explanation: Agreeing on a party is not agreeing on a place. Settling who chooses comes before anyone's favorite venue. Leaving her to it assumes you both picture the same party, which is how hurt starts.

questions.prompt: Two neighbors chat over their shared fence and agree it needs replacing. That evening, one hires a company and slides half the bill under the other's door. The other is angry. Where was the trap?
choices: Thinking one short chat over the fence was enough time to talk it through.
Thinking a yes to a new fence meant a yes to that company.
Thinking a note under the door was fine for the bill.
questions.explanation: Agreeing the fence needs replacing said nothing about who hires whom. Naming who chooses the company would have prevented the surprise bill. More talk about the fence would not, since they already agreed on it.

questions.prompt: After a tense talk about the Mother's Day window, a florist tells her two staff, "Send me your ideas by Wednesday, then I'll choose." What most likely happens next?
choices: One of them may not love the pick, but nobody feels misled.
The staff feel shut out, since only the florist gets the final say.
The staff argue on until Wednesday, since nothing is settled yet.
questions.explanation: Everyone knew the florist would choose after hearing their ideas, so the result matches what they expected. Hearing ideas first, then deciding alone, is one of the four ways, and it settles the question.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My business partner and I agreed we need a bigger delivery van. Now we argue every night about which one." What do you suggest?
choices: Ask your accountant to check first that a bigger van is really worth it.
Agree first whether one of you picks or you both must say yes.
Each write down what you need from a van, then compare lists.
questions.explanation: They agreed on needing a van but never said how they would choose one. Settling that ends the nightly fight. Comparing lists adds more views but still names nobody to decide, so the arguing goes on.

questions.prompt: Staff at a climbing gym argue about which wall to rebuild first. Before leaving, they agree to settle it by a show of hands at Monday's meeting. The losing side grumbles but goes along. Why did it hold?
choices: Everyone knew before the vote how the choice would be made.
A show of hands is the fairest way for groups to decide.
The days before Monday let everyone cool down first.
questions.explanation: The losing side knew the rule before the vote, so the result did not feel like a trick. A show of hands is not the fairest way everywhere. It held because everyone agreed to it ahead of time.

reviewCards.front: Your team agreed the office needed a new layout. One Monday you arrive to find every desk moved, and half the team feels ignored. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The talk ended on a shared yes, but nobody said who would choose the new layout or how. Each person pictured having a say.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should happen before a talk that ended in agreement breaks up?
reviewCards.back: Someone says out loud who makes the final choice and how: one person alone, one person after hearing others, a vote, or everyone agreeing.

reviewCards.front: You and your partner agree the living room needs a new sofa. That evening your partner opens a furniture website. What do you say?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether one of you chooses after hearing the other, or you both have to say yes to the same sofa before anyone pays.

reviewCards.front: Why can a talk where everyone nodded leave someone feeling let down a week later?
reviewCards.back: Each person nodded to a different picture of what came next. With nobody named to decide, one person acts and the others feel their trust was broken.

reviewCards.front: When a hard talk finally ends with everyone nodding, the last thing to say out loud is ...
reviewCards.back: ... who will make the final choice and which way it gets made, so nobody leaves guessing.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Turning a shared yes into a clear plan for who chooses and how, before everyone leaves.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I end a meeting or call where we agreed on something, I name who makes the final choice and which of the four ways we use, before anyone leaves.
When I notice a talk ending in nods with nobody named to decide, I ask out loud who makes the final choice, and whether they decide alone, after hearing us, by vote, or with everyone agreeing.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next talk today that ends in agreement, be the one who asks who makes the final choice and how, before anyone stands up.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of one regular meeting or family plan each week, ask who decides and how. Later in the week, notice whether anyone was surprised by what got done.

chapters.title: Talking With Someone You Don't Trust
chapters.hook: Freeze out the coworker you don't trust, and the plan gets made without you. Trust them on this one plan, and you're in the room.
chapters.counterintuition: You can't talk with someone you don't trust, because they'll twist whatever you say. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: trust is not all or nothing. You only need enough trust for the one issue in front of you.
chapters.keyTakeaway: You can hold a real talk with someone you don't trust by trusting them on just this one issue.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tonight, write down one thing you must settle with someone you don't trust, and what you can count on them for on it.

memorableLines.text: Doubt them on everything else if you must, but trust them on this one thing.

breakdown.fastRead:
Three offers have come in on Nadia's late father's house, and the agent wants an answer by Friday. She and her brother Ezra must agree on one, and she hasn't trusted him since he never paid back money their dad lent him. She plans to say nothing until he gives in. If they haven't agreed by Friday, the best buyer walks away.

Silence feels safe, but it treats trust as all or nothing. Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler say it isn't. You can trust a coworker's word on a deadline and still never lend them money. So you only need enough trust for the issue in front of you. Ask what you can count on them for on that point. Then start from a mutual purpose, a goal you both want, and leave old fights out.

That evening Nadia calls Ezra. She doesn't trust him with money, but she trusts him to want a good price, since half of it is his. She says she isn't calling about the loan, only to pick the best offer for Dad's house. They pick one before the call ends. The loan still sits between them. When you must talk with someone you don't trust, trust them on just this one issue, and the talk can get somewhere.

Underneath her plan is the idea that trust is all or nothing, so a person you doubt in one place can't be dealt with anywhere. You might take a coworker's word on a deadline and still never lend them money. So you don't need to trust a person in everything. You need enough trust for the issue in front of you.

That turns a stuck talk into a small question. On this one point, what can you count on them for? Often the answer is what they want. Start there, with a mutual purpose, a goal you both really share on that point. Then make it safe by keeping old fights out of this talk, so the other person doesn't brace for an attack. The bigger doubts don't vanish. They just stop blocking the one thing you have to settle today.

That evening Nadia calls Ezra. She still doesn't trust him with money. She does trust him to want a good price, since half of it is his. She says she isn't calling about the loan, only to pick the best offer for Dad's house. He's quiet for a moment, then starts comparing the numbers with her. They pick one before the call ends. breakdown.fullRead:
Three offers have come in on Nadia's late father's house, and the agent wants an answer by Friday. She and her brother Ezra must agree on one, and she hasn't trusted him since he never paid back money their dad lent him. She tells herself he'll twist anything she says. So she plans to say nothing until he gives in. If they haven't agreed by Friday, the best buyer walks away. The house would sit empty through the winter, with its bills still coming.

Her plan makes sense to her. Talking feels like handing Ezra one more chance to hurt her. But silence protects nothing here. Ezra can't read her mind, the agent can't choose for them, and Friday keeps coming. Her other choice looks no better. She could open the call with the loan and finally let him have it. Then the talk would be about the old hurt, and the house would still be stuck.

Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler studied moments like this, where the stakes are high, views differ and feelings run strong. Most people, they found, fall into silence or violence. Silence means holding back what you really think. Violence means pushing your view with blame, labels or force. Nadia is about to do the first and is tempted by the second. The authors' answer is that handling these moments well is a skill you can learn, not a gift.

People who learn these skills often push back that their own case is different. The authors work through those cases one by one, and one comes up all the time: people say they can't talk with someone because they don't trust them. It sounds like the end of the matter. Their answer is that the same tools still apply, because trust is not all or nothing.

You can trust a person in one area and not in another. Think of a coworker whose word on a deadline you'd take without a second thought. You might still never lend that coworker money. Both judgments are fair, and they sit side by side. So you don't need to trust someone in everything. You only need enough trust for the issue in front of you.

That turns a stuck talk into a small, clear question. On this one point, what can you count on them for? Often the answer is what they want. A person you doubt with money may still want a good price, a calm week or a happy child, just as you do. Start there, with a mutual purpose, a goal you both really share on that point. Then make it safe. Keep old fights out of this talk and tell them so, and they won't have to brace for an attack.

None of this asks you to forget what happened. The bigger doubts stay where they are. You aren't handing the person your trust in everything. You are giving it on one issue, for one talk, because that issue matters to you both. The doubt that once shut the talk down now simply sits beside it.

That evening Nadia calls Ezra. She still doesn't trust him with money. She does trust him to want a good price, since half of it is his. She says she isn't calling about the loan, only to pick the best offer for Dad's house. He's quiet for a moment. Then he starts comparing the numbers with her. They pick one before the call ends. The loan still sits between them. When you must talk with someone you don't trust, trust them only on the question at hand, and the talk can get somewhere.

examples.title: The friend who left you the hotel bill
examples.scenario: Kenji and Lars have been friends since school, but after a trip last spring, Lars left Kenji with the whole hotel bill and never paid his half. Now their friend Sunny turns forty next month, and Lars wants to plan a surprise party together. Kenji sits in his car outside the gym, reading the message, his thumb over the reply box.
examples.whatToDo: Say yes to building the guest list with Lars, who knows Sunny's friends best, and keep the deposit on your own card.
examples.whyItMatters: Sunny gets a party both friends built, and Kenji never has to trust Lars with cash to make it happen.

examples.title: Two florists talking through the owner
examples.scenario: At a small flower shop, Amara opens and Pieter closes. Since Pieter blamed her for a lost delivery in March, she passes everything to him through the owner instead of talking. Last Saturday a wedding order for white roses got placed twice, and the shop lost three hundred dollars of flowers. The owner told them both, "Sort this out between yourselves."
examples.whatToDo: Catch Pieter at the shift change and talk about orders only, trusting that he wants every wedding to go right as much as she does.
examples.whyItMatters: The old blame can wait. One shared goal on orders stops the double buying and gives the owner two staff who talk.

examples.title: Spelling words at the weekend handover
examples.scenario: Valeria is quizzing her son Felix on spelling words at the coffee table when his dad, Dominic, arrives early for the weekend handover. She stopped counting on Dominic after he missed two of Felix's games. Still, she asks him to go over the list with Felix on Saturday. He folds his arms. "So now you're checking up on me?"
examples.whatToDo: Leave the missed games out of it. Say plainly that he wants Felix to pass too, and ask how he'd like to practice the list.
examples.whyItMatters: Dominic stops guarding himself and starts helping, and Felix gets spelling practice at both homes, whatever his parents still doubt about each other.

questions.prompt: A food truck worker doesn't trust her coworker, who once blamed her for a burnt order. She asks him only about splitting the prep, since they both want a calm lunch rush. They settle it in ten minutes. Why did the talk go so smoothly?
choices: She only had to trust him on the prep, not on everything.
Keeping the talk short left neither of them time to fight.
She let him feel in charge of the prep, so he went along.
questions.explanation: She still doubts him, but she could count on him to want a calm lunch rush, and that was enough to settle the prep. The short talk came from that. It wasn't the reason.

questions.prompt: Your upstairs neighbor once told the landlord you were subletting, which was false. Now the building's heating keeps cutting out, and you two need to agree on what to tell the repair company. What do you do?
choices: Wait until he admits the subletting lie before working with him.
Talk with him about the heating, since you both want warm flats.
Raise the subletting story first, so it's out of the way before the heating.
questions.explanation: You don't need to trust him in everything, only on the heating, and he wants a warm flat as much as you do. Raising the old story first turns a repair talk into the old fight.

questions.prompt: A running club captain needs the treasurer to book a van for next month's race. Last year she lost some of the entry fees. He thinks, "Why bother asking? She'll twist it." Where does his thinking go wrong?
choices: He is judging the treasurer harshly over one old mistake.
He thinks he must trust the treasurer in everything to ask.
He forgot to raise the lost fees before asking about the van.
questions.explanation: He can doubt her with money and still trust her to want the club at the race. That's enough to ask about a van. Raising the lost fees first would bury the van under last year's trouble.

questions.prompt: Two gym trainers share a Saturday class. Last month one took a client from the other. Before class, the trainer who lost the client says, "Let's leave the client thing aside today. We both want this class full. Can we split warm-up and weights?" What most likely happens?
choices: Her coworker hears an accusation about the client and walks off angry.
They split the class, and the old grudge is gone.
They plan the class together, and the client issue stays open.
questions.explanation: She kept the talk on one goal they share, a full class, and left the old fight out, so it felt safe enough to plan. That doesn't settle the client problem. The bigger doubt is still there afterward.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My sister-in-law gossips about me, so I won't talk to her about who hosts the holidays this year. She'll twist it." What's your best reply?
choices: "You don't need to trust her with secrets to plan one dinner."
"Ask your partner to handle it, since she's their sister."
"Give her a clean slate this year and let the old gossip go."
questions.explanation: Your friend can stay careful with secrets and still trust the sister-in-law to want a good holiday. A clean slate asks for far more trust than planning one dinner needs.

questions.prompt: A landscaping crew lead doesn't trust a worker who once padded his hours. Before a big job she tells him, "Today is about the stone wall. We both want it finished before the rain." He then mentions a drainage problem he spotted. What made him open up?
choices: Naming the wall gave them one goal they both cared about.
He wanted to make up for padding his hours.
The coming rain made the job too urgent for either to argue.
questions.explanation: She didn't need to trust him on hours, only on the wall, and he wanted it finished too. The rain was coming either way. The shared goal is what made the drainage problem worth raising.

questions.prompt: You and a coworker share a client. Last year she took credit for your report. Now your boss wants you two to agree who presents which part of next week's pitch. What's your next step?
choices: Send her an email with the split, so there's a record you can point to.
Let her choose the split this time, just to keep the peace.
Sit with her and agree on the split, since you both want the client.
questions.explanation: You only need to trust her on this pitch, and she wants to win the client too. An email might feel safer, but it skips the talk where you two actually agree.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what can you do when you must talk with someone you don't trust?
reviewCards.back: Pick the one issue you need to settle and trust them on that alone, starting from a goal you both want. The bigger doubts can stay.

reviewCards.front: A coworker once read your private messages on a shared screen. Now the two of you must swap shifts over the holidays. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Talk with them about the shift swap only. You can still doubt them on privacy and trust them to want a fair holiday.

reviewCards.front: Why can you talk with someone you distrust without fixing the whole relationship first?
reviewCards.back: Because trust isn't all or nothing. You can doubt someone in one area and still count on them in the one you're deciding today.

reviewCards.front: When you don't trust someone but must settle something with them, you only need ...
reviewCards.back: ... enough trust for that one thing, such as what you both want from it, while the bigger doubts wait.

reviewCards.front: Two flatmates had to decide on replacing their broken fridge. One opened by listing every bill the other had paid late. They never got to the fridge. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The talk tried to settle all the distrust at once. Trusting the flatmate on the fridge alone, since both want cold food, would have let them decide.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Narrowing your trust to the single matter at hand, so doubt about the person stops blocking the talk.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking there's no point talking to someone, I name the one issue we must settle and what I can count on them for there.
When I sit down across from someone I don't fully trust, I open with the goal we both want on today's issue and leave old fights out.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, pick one person you don't fully trust and one thing you must settle with them. Say out loud what you can count on them for on that thing alone.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time this week you put off a talk because you don't trust someone, ask what you can count on them for on that one matter. Then have the talk about that matter only.
